question: Where can a mathematical object stop behaving smoothly?
idea: A solution or shape may be well-behaved in some places and irregular in others. Understanding those irregularities helps distinguish a controlled solution from a possible breakdown. This entry studies the particular situation described below.
why: The study of equations that describe how quantities vary across space and time, such as waves, fluids, and heat.

glossary.meaning: A way of measuring how much of a larger set is occupied; the particular counting convention matters.
A family of probability distributions and random fields generalizing the familiar bell curve.
A place where an object or solution fails to have the expected smooth or regular behavior.
A bound or statement whose control does not deteriorate across the specified range of inputs.
A way of measuring the number of independent directions or degrees of freedom; different theories use different notions.

exactClaim: Derives the nonlinear Boltzmann equation from three-dimensional grand-canonical Newtonian gases throughout every regular kinetic interval with uniform Gaussian decay. Stable finite-range radial potentials may have attractive wells and a singular repulsive core; initial pair exclusion and spatially summable Gaussian density and gradient bounds are assumed. A companion gives finite-dimensional hard-sphere Gaussian fluctuations, centered at the exact microscopic expectation and governed by the linear fluctuating Boltzmann equation.
scope: A definition-led reading guide; the exact mathematical claim is preserved separately. This is not a proof assessment.
